Order matters — canonical links and search run last Search builds its index from the final state of every page, so it has to run after everything else. Canonical links have to come after plugin-tags too, or the tag pages it generates get no canonical link — and alphabetically, canonical-links would run before tags. config/plugin-order.yaml says so: plugin-order: - end: - plugin-canonical-links - plugin-search Everything else runs alphabetically in between. This is the one place plugin ordering is load-bearing on this site. Templates we own Plugins that ship views were published into theme/views/vendor/ with commands like npx nera-navigation. Today npx nera add <name> runs that command for you, in the same step as the install and the copy of the plugin's default config. Those copies are ours to edit and style — nothing important is hidden inside node_modules. Content is just Markdown Every page you're reading is a Markdown file under pages/ with a layout in its frontmatter. The docs are pages/docs/*.md; this tutorial is pages/tutorials/how-this-site-is-built.md. Folders become URLs; no routing config exists. Build npm run build # pages/ -> public/ Checks and deploy Every push to main and every pull request against it runs .github/workflows/test.yml on Node 22 and 24 — the same commands you can run locally: npm ci npm run lint # eslint npm test # node --test on the local plugins' and scripts' tests npm run validate # nera validate: layouts, includes, frontmatter npm run build -- --check # nera build --check --check looks at the built public/ for accessibility, privacy and legal-notice problems and reports what it finds. Findings are warnings, so they fail the run only for a rule that config/validate.yaml promotes to an error. A push to main then runs .github/workflows/deploy.yml: npm ci, npm run build, then npm run build:demos and npm run check:demos, which build and check the blog theme demos under /themes/blog/ from the starters' latest releases. public/ is then published to GitHub Pages — the site you are reading at nera.js.org. That's the entire stack: Markdown in, static HTML out, plugins for the rest. If you've read the other tutorials in this section, you've now seen every piece of it in isolation — this is just all of them together.

title: Tutorials
description: Step-by-step guides for building real sites with Nera and its plugins.
content: Hands-on guides for building real things with Nera — from a first blog to wiring up individual plugins. Browse by topic below, or read the latest.

title: Build a one-page site
description: A single scrolling landing page from one Markdown file per section, with an in-page navigation, a mailto contact form and social links in the footer.
content: A freelancer or a small business often needs one page, not a site: a hero, the services, a few words about who you are, and a way to get in touch, all on one scrolling page. In this tutorial you build that page with each section in its own Markdown file. @nera-static/plugin-one-page merges the sections into the home page, @nera-static/plugin-page-navigation adds the in-page links, @nera-static/plugin-contact-form adds a contact form without a backend, and @nera-static/plugin-social-media-links puts your profiles in the footer. Want a finished business site to edit instead? The business starter sets one up with a theme, sample pages for services, about, opening hours and contact, a contact form and social links: npx @nera-static/nera new my-site --starter business Its files won't match the steps below: the starter builds a site of several pages, while this tutorial builds a single page by hand, to show how the pieces fit together. 1. Scaffold and install npx @nera-static/nera new my-site cd my-site npx nera add one-page npx nera add page-navigation npx nera add contact-form npx nera add social-media-links nera add takes one plugin per call. Each call installs the package, which Nera then finds on its own, and copies the plugin's default config into config/. Three of the four ship templates, and nera add publishes them into theme/views/vendor/plugin-<name>/, where they are yours to edit. The contact form's client script lands in theme/assets/js/contact-form.js. plugin-one-page ships no template. Its copied config/one-page.yaml only names the frontmatter keys it reads (add_to_page, add_to_page_order, anchor_id and the others). Leave it as it is, and config/page-navigation.yaml too, which sets the class of the active link. Steps 7 and 8 replace the other two files. 2. The target page The page the sections are merged into is an ordinary page. Here it is the home page, and its own content is the hero: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug title: Studio Lena description: Web design for small businesses in Berlin --- # Websites for small businesses I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices. Give it a template of its own. It grows in the next steps; for now it renders the content: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content 3. One file per section Each section is a Markdown file that names its target page in add_to_page and its position in add_to_page_order. Keep them together in pages/sections/: --- title: Services add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 1 anchor_id: services content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--services --- ## Services - **New websites**: from the first sketch to the live site. - **Redesigns**: a fresh look for the site you already have. - **Care plans**: updates and small changes every month. --- title: About add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 2 anchor_id: about content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--about --- ## About I'm Lena, a web designer in Berlin. I have built sites for small businesses since 2015. --- title: Contact add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 3 anchor_id: contact content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--contact --- ## Contact Tell me about your project. The form opens your own email program with the message ready to send. Run npx nera build. Until step 7 it also warns that plugin-contact-form has no recipient configured; the form simply does not render yet. public/index.html now holds the hero followed by the three sections, in their order (shortened): <main id="main"> <h1>Websites for small businesses</h1> <p>I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices.</p> <section class="section section--services"> <a id="services"></a> <h2>Services</h2> <ul> <li><strong>New websites</strong>: from the first sketch to the live site.</li> … </ul> </section> <section class="section section--about"> <a id="about"></a> <h2>About</h2> … </section> <section class="section section--contact"> <a id="contact"></a> <h2>Contact</h2> … </section> </main> The sections are always appended after the target page's own content. Each one is wrapped in a <section>; content_wrapper_tag sets another element, and content_wrapper_tag: '' drops the wrapper. The wrapper attributes are a plain mapping or a list of { attribute, value } entries, and their values are HTML-escaped. Quote a value that contains : : content_wrapper_attributes: style: 'background-color: #f5f5f5;' Unquoted, the frontmatter does not parse: the build logs ❌ Failed to process page …: Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings …, drops the page and still exits 0. nera validate reports it as a yaml-parse error. add_to_page must match exactly add_to_page is compared literally with the target page's href, which always starts with / and ends in .html: pages/index.md is /index.html, pages/de/index.md is /de/index.html. With add_to_page: index.html nothing is merged, and the build says so: ⚠️ one-page: no page has href "index.html" — 1 section(s) targeting it were not merged. `add_to_page` must match a page's href exactly, e.g. "/index.html" for pages/index.md 4. Anchors Each section gets an empty <a id="…"> in front of its content, so /index.html#services jumps to it. anchor_id sets the id. Without it, the plugin derives one from the section's first <h1>, slugified: lowercase, accents removed, everything else turned into -. This section has no anchor_id: --- title: Team add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 4 --- # Über uns Zwei Leute, ein Studio. It is merged as: <section> <a id="uber-uns"></a> <h1>Über uns</h1> <p>Zwei Leute, ein Studio.</p> </section> Lower headings are ignored, so a section with only ## headings gets no anchor unless you set anchor_id. And an <h1> per section is not what you want on a one-page site: the home page already has its <h1>, and with team.md in place nera build --check warns page has more than one `<h1>` (a11y-h1). So give the sections ## headings and an explicit anchor_id, as in step 3, and delete team.md again. Explicit ids also stay the same when you rename a heading or translate the page (see step 10). 5. Sections without a page of their own A section is still a page of its own. Nera writes a page only if it has a layout, and the sections above have none, so they exist only inside /index.html. Add layout: pages/default.pug to about.md and the build also writes /sections/about.html, while the section still appears on the home page. Leave layout out unless you want that second URL. nera validate does not know that the missing layout is on purpose: pages/sections/about.md :1 warning page has no `layout` — the build skips it silently; add `layout: pages/default.pug` to its frontmatter (a template in theme/views), or, if it has none on purpose (a fragment or draft), add `ignore: { layout-missing: [pages/sections/about.md] }` to config/validate.yaml layout-missing … 0 error(s), 3 warning(s) Because all sections live in one folder, one entry silences them all: ignore: layout-missing: - pages/sections A folder covers everything below it. nera validate now prints ✓ No problems found. 6. In-page navigation plugin-page-navigation builds a navigation of sibling pages in the same folder, and skips pages at the site root, so on its own it gives index.md nothing. Its other mode fits: a page_navigation list in the page's frontmatter, whose entries go to the template exactly as written. Point them at the anchors: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug title: Studio Lena description: Web design for small businesses in Berlin page_navigation: - href: '#services' name: Services - href: '#about' name: About - href: '#contact' name: Contact --- # Websites for small businesses I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices. Quote the hrefs: in YAML an unquoted # after a space starts a comment. Include the published template above the content: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main include /vendor/plugin-page-navigation/page-navigation != content The <nav> is named by the translation key Page navigation, so it stays distinct from a main menu for screen readers. Give it a label in your language in config/app.yaml: translations: en: Page navigation: On this page The built page starts with: <nav class="page-nav" aria-label="On this page"><a class="page-nav__link" href="#services">Services</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#about">About</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#contact">Contact</a></nav> You could write these three links into the template by hand just as well. The plugin earns its place once the links differ per page or per language: they live in each page's frontmatter, next to the content they point to. 7. The contact form plugin-contact-form renders a form from config/contact-form.yaml. The copy nera add made documents every key, with the recipient commented out and a set of sample fields; replace it with this one. On submit a small script in the browser builds a mailto: link from the fields and opens the visitor's own email program with subject and message filled in. There is no backend: your site stores and sends nothing, and the message leaves only through the visitor's email. (Handling the form on a server is not covered here.) recipient: hello@example.com subject: contact_subject submit_label: contact_submit error_required: contact_required error_email: contact_email_invalid fields: - { name: name, label: contact_name, type: text, required: true } - { name: email, label: contact_email, type: email, required: true } - name: topic label: contact_topic type: select required: true options: - { value: new-site, label: contact_topic_new } - { value: redesign, label: contact_topic_redesign } - { value: care, label: contact_topic_care } - { name: message, label: contact_message, type: textarea, required: true } Every user-facing value here is a translation key, resolved for each page's language from translations: in config/app.yaml. A key without a translation renders as written, so a site in one language could write the text directly; keys pay off in step 10. name and the option values are data and are never translated. Add the English texts: translations: en: Page navigation: On this page contact_subject: Enquiry from the website contact_submit: Open in my email program contact_required: Please fill in all required fields. contact_email_invalid: Please enter a valid email address. contact_name: Your name contact_email: Your email contact_topic: What can I help with? contact_topic_new: A new website contact_topic_redesign: A redesign contact_topic_care: A care plan contact_message: Your message Keep the keys nera new put under en: (app_description, skip_to_content and the others) next to these. The form is Pug, so it goes in the template, not in a Markdown section. The contact section has the highest add_to_page_order, so the form placed after the content follows its text directly: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main include /vendor/plugin-page-navigation/page-navigation != content include /vendor/plugin-contact-form/contact-form The built form (shortened): <form class="contact-form" novalidate="novalidate" data-contact-form="data-contact-form"> <script type="application/json" data-contact-config="data-contact-config"> { "subject": "Enquiry from the website", … } </script><span class="contact-form__recipient" hidden="hidden" data-contact-recipient="&#104;&#101;&#108;&#108;&#111;&#64;&#101;&#120;&#97;&#109;&#112;&#108;&#101;&#46;&#99;&#111;&#109;"></span> <div class="contact-form__field contact-form__field--text"><label class="contact-form__label" for="contact-name">Your name</label><input class="contact-form__input" type="text" id="contact-name" name="name" data-contact-field="data-contact-field" data-contact-label="Your name" required="required" /></div> … <div class="contact-form__decoy" aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:-9999px;top:auto;width:1px;height:1px;overflow:hidden"><label for="contact-website">website</label><input type="text" id="contact-website" name="website" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off" /></div> <div class="contact-form__status" role="alert" aria-live="polite" data-contact-status="data-contact-status"></div><button class="contact-form__submit" type="submit">Open in my email program</button> </form> <script src="/js/contact-form.js"></script> Submitted with every field filled in, the form opened this link: mailto:hello@example.com?subject=Enquiry%20from%20the%20website&body=Your%20name%3A%20Jane%20Doe%0D%0AYour%20email%3A%20jane%40example.org%0D%0AWhat%20can%20I%20help%20with%3F%3A%20redesign%0D%0AYour%20message%3A%20Hello%20Lena Submitted empty, it opened nothing and showed Please fill in all required fields. in the status line. Three details are worth knowing: The recipient is obfuscated, not hidden. It never appears as readable text, but it is in the page: obfuscation What lands in the HTML Strength entities (default) each character as an HTML entity, as above deters naïve scrapers; a determined one can still decode it jsassembly only an array of character codes, rebuilt in JavaScript on submit stronger, still not a guarantee Use an address you are willing to publish. A honeypot is built in. The hidden website field is a decoy for bots; a submission that fills it is dropped silently. Never give a real field the honeypot's name. If you want a real "website" field, rename the decoy with honeypot: in the config. The plugin ships no CSS apart from the inline rule that hides the decoy. Style the BEM classes .contact-form, .contact-form__field, .contact-form__input and the others from your own stylesheet. 8. Social links in the footer plugin-social-media-links reads a list of links from config/social-media-links.yaml. In the copy nera add made, the list is a commented-out example, so nothing renders yet. Replace the file with: aria_label: Social media open_in_new_tab: false social_media_links: - name: GitHub href: https://github.com/yourname icon: '<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 .297c-6.63 0-12 5.373-12 12 …"/></svg>' icon_raw: true - name: LinkedIn href: https://www.linkedin.com/in/yourname The d attribute is shortened here; paste the full path of the icon you use. Simple Icons (simpleicons.org) has brand logos as SVG. icon is escaped unless the entry sets icon_raw: true, so set it only for markup you wrote or checked yourself. The LinkedIn entry has no icon and shows its name only. The example list in the copied config uses Font Awesome <i> tags instead, which need the Font Awesome CSS. Loading it from a CDN sends every visitor's IP address to a third party, and nera build --check then warns privacy-third-party. Inline SVG or plain text needs no request at all. open_in_new_tab: false lets the visitor decide where a link opens; without it, every link gets target="_blank". rel="noopener noreferrer" is set either way. Include the published template in the footer of the base layout that nera new created. Remove its first line, the //- nera:scaffold-default marker, now that the file is your own: <!DOCTYPE html> html(lang=app.lang) head meta(charset="UTF-8") meta(name="viewport", content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0") title #{ meta.title } | #{ app.name } meta(name="description", content=`${ meta.description || t('app_description') }`) meta(name="keywords", content=`${ meta.keywords || t('app_keywords') }`) meta(name="generator" content="nera") meta(name="robots" content=`${ meta.robots || app.robots }`) style. .skip-link { position: absolute; left: -9999px; } .skip-link:focus { position: static; } body a.skip-link(href="#main") #{ t('skip_to_content') } block content footer include /vendor/plugin-social-media-links/social-media-links a(href="/imprint.html") #{ t('imprint') } = ' · ' a(href="/privacy.html") #{ t('privacy') } The footer now starts with (SVG path shortened): <footer> <nav class="social-media-links" aria-label="Social media"> <ul class="social-media-links__list"> <li class="social-media-links__item"><a class="social-media-links__link" href="https://github.com/yourname" title="GitHub" rel="noopener noreferrer"><span class="social-media-links__icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 .297c-6.63 0-12 5.373-12 12 …"/></svg></span><span class="social-media-links__label">GitHub</span></a></li> <li class="social-media-links__item"><a class="social-media-links__link" href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/yourname" title="LinkedIn" rel="noopener noreferrer"><span class="social-media-links__icon"></span><span class="social-media-links__label">LinkedIn</span></a></li> </ul> </nav><a href="/imprint.html">Imprint</a> · <a href="/privacy.html">Privacy</a> </footer> 9. Scrolling under a sticky navigation A little CSS makes the page feel like one: the navigation stays at the top, the links scroll smoothly, and a section does not end up hidden under the navigation. Create theme/assets/css/site.css: html { scroll-behavior: smooth; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto; } } .page-nav { position: sticky; top: 0; display: flex; gap: 1rem; padding: 1rem 0; background: #fff; } .section > a[id] { scroll-margin-top: 4rem; } The scroll target is the anchor, not the <section>, so scroll-margin-top goes on a[id]. Load the file in the layout's head, after the meta lines: link(rel="stylesheet", href="/css/site.css") Files in theme/assets/ are served from the site root, so the file is /css/site.css. In a headless browser, on a page long enough to scroll that far, a click on each navigation link put its heading 64 px (4rem) from the top, just below the 50 px high sticky navigation. 10. A second language A German copy of the page is a second target with its own sections. Set lang: de on each file and target /de/index.html: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug lang: de title: Studio Lena description: Webdesign für kleine Unternehmen in Berlin page_navigation: - href: '#services' name: Leistungen - href: '#about' name: Über mich - href: '#contact' name: Kontakt --- # Websites für kleine Unternehmen Ich gestalte und baue schnelle, einfache Websites für Läden, Studios und Praxen. --- lang: de title: Leistungen add_to_page: /de/index.html add_to_page_order: 1 anchor_id: services content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--services --- ## Leistungen - **Neue Websites**: von der ersten Skizze bis zur fertigen Seite. - **Redesigns**: ein frischer Auftritt für die Website, die Sie schon haben. - **Pflege**: Updates und kleine Änderungen jeden Monat. about.md and contact.md in pages/de/sections/ follow the same pattern with anchor_id: about and anchor_id: contact. The anchors stay the same in both languages, so the CSS works for both and a link to #contact works on either page. Extend the ignore entry to every language folder; * stands for one folder name: ignore: layout-missing: - pages/sections - pages/*/sections Translate the keys from steps 6 and 7 under de: in config/app.yaml: de: app_description: Eine statische Website, gebaut mit Nera app_keywords: nera, static site generator skip_to_content: Zum Inhalt springen imprint: Impressum privacy: Datenschutz Page navigation: Auf dieser Seite contact_subject: Anfrage über die Website contact_submit: In meinem E-Mail-Programm öffnen contact_required: Bitte füllen Sie alle Pflichtfelder aus. contact_email_invalid: Bitte geben Sie eine gültige E-Mail-Adresse ein. contact_name: Ihr Name contact_email: Ihre E-Mail-Adresse contact_topic: Wobei kann ich helfen? contact_topic_new: Eine neue Website contact_topic_redesign: Ein Redesign contact_topic_care: Ein Pflegepaket contact_message: Ihre Nachricht The scaffolded layout sets html(lang=app.lang), which is en on every page. Use the page's language instead: html(lang=meta.lang || app.lang) /de/index.html then has <html lang="de">, the German navigation and the German form, with the same field names: <nav class="page-nav" aria-label="Auf dieser Seite"><a class="page-nav__link" href="#services">Leistungen</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#about">Über mich</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#contact">Kontakt</a></nav> … <div class="contact-form__field contact-form__field--text"><label class="contact-form__label" for="contact-name">Ihr Name</label><input class="contact-form__input" type="text" id="contact-name" name="name" data-contact-field="data-contact-field" data-contact-label="Ihr Name" required="required" /></div> The social links' aria_label is not passed through t() by the shipped template. To translate it, change the nav line in your published theme/views/vendor/plugin-social-media-links/social-media-links.pug: nav.social-media-links(aria-label=t(app.socialMediaLinksLabel)) and add Social media: Soziale Medien under de:. With all of this in place, nera validate and nera build --check both print ✓ No problems found. One page or stacks? plugin-stacks also turns Markdown files into pieces of other pages, but the other way round. A stack is a block that a view places, anywhere and as often as you like, through app.stacks; it marks itself with type: stack and needs no validate.yaml entry. A one-page section names its target page in add_to_page, and the plugin appends it to that page's content, in order, with an anchor and a wrapper, without touching a template. Use one-page when a page is a sequence of sections. Use stacks when the same block belongs in several places or in a particular spot of a layout. Next Build a navigation with active states adds a main menu, once the one page grows into a few. How this website is built shows a complete Nera site with its plugins working together.

title: Add prev/next links between pages
description: Use plugin-page-pagination to link sibling pages in reading order.
content: @nera-static/plugin-page-pagination links each page to its previous and next sibling — pages in the same directory — in an order you control. Perfect for docs and multi-part tutorials. 1. Install and publish the template npx nera add page-pagination nera add installs the package, copies its config/page-pagination.yaml into your site and publishes the template into theme/views/vendor/plugin-page-pagination/. The defaults need no setting, so the one key in that file is commented out. 2. Order the pages By default the plugin reads a pagination_order number from each page: --- title: Getting started pagination_order: 2 --- Pages are ordered by pagination_order first, then by creation date, then by path — so a page without an explicit order still lands somewhere stable. Ordering starts at 0 if you want it to: the plugin treats 0 as a real value, not "missing". To read a different key, uncomment order_property in config/page-pagination.yaml and set its name. 3. Render the links The plugin adds meta.pagePagination with .previous and .next. Include the published template, guarded so it's hidden when there's nowhere to go: if meta.pagePagination && (meta.pagePagination.previous || meta.pagePagination.next) include ../vendor/plugin-page-pagination/page-pagination Why "siblings only" matters Pagination is scoped per directory, so pages/docs/*.md paginate among themselves and pages/tutorials/*.md among themselves — they never bleed into each other. Put a sequence in its own folder and it just works. This site's docs use exactly this.

title: Responsive images with plugin-images
description: Turn the photos in your Markdown into AVIF and WebP with srcset, sizes, width and height at build time, with camera and GPS data stripped, and cache the work between builds.
content: A photo straight from a camera or a phone is several megabytes and thousands of pixels wide, and it carries metadata: the camera model, the time, often the GPS position where it was taken. Put it into a Markdown page as it is, and every visitor downloads all of that, on a phone too. @nera-static/plugin-images fixes this at build time. Every local image in your Markdown becomes a <picture> with AVIF and WebP in several widths, srcset/sizes, width/height and lazy loading, and the published files carry no metadata. Your Markdown does not change. Every command, config and output below was run in a fresh nera new site with plugin-images 1.0.3, @nera-static/core 4.18.3 and @nera-static/nera 1.27.2. The photo is a 4000 × 3000 JPEG of 4 MB with camera and GPS data in its EXIF block. 1. Install npx nera add images nera add installs the package and publishes the plugin's one view, the picture mixin, into theme/views/vendor/plugin-images/: ✅ Copied picture.pug to …/theme/views/vendor/plugin-images/picture.pug ✅ Templates copied to: …/theme/views/vendor/plugin-images ✅ Added @nera-static/plugin-images Config: none (the plugin ships no default) Templates: published by the plugin There is nothing else to set up: a config/images.yaml is optional, and so is every key in it. Every official starter except blank (nera new --starter …) already ships the plugin. 2. Before and after Put the photo into the site's assets, at theme/assets/images/photos/pier.jpg, and use it in a page like any image: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: The pier description: A photo of the pier at dusk --- # The pier ![The pier at dusk, seen from the beach](/images/photos/pier.jpg) Without the plugin, nera build turns this into a plain <img> that points at the 4 MB original: <p><img src="/images/photos/pier.jpg" alt="The pier at dusk, seen from the beach"></p> With the plugin, the first build encodes the variants: 🖼️ plugin-images: 1 image(s), 12 variant(s) encoded and public/pier.html holds: <p> <picture> <source type="image/avif" srcset="/_img/pier-1a5869e3-480.avif 480w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-800.avif 800w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-1200.avif 1200w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-1600.avif 1600w" sizes="100vw"> <source type="image/webp" srcset="/_img/pier-987422b0-480.webp 480w, /_img/pier-987422b0-800.webp 800w, /_img/pier-987422b0-1200.webp 1200w, /_img/pier-987422b0-1600.webp 1600w" sizes="100vw"><img src="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-480.jpg 480w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-800.jpg 800w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1200.jpg 1200w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="100vw" width="1600" height="1200" alt="The pier at dusk, seen from the beach" loading="eager" fetchpriority="high"> </picture> </p> The browser picks the first format it supports, AVIF, then WebP, and the <img> is the fallback. It keeps the source's format (JPEG stays JPEG, PNG stays PNG) and always points at a processed variant, never the original. The widths are the default 480, 800, 1200, 1600. A source is never upscaled: a photo 1000 pixels wide gets 480 and 800 only. width and height are the largest variant's size, so the browser reserves the space before the image loads and the page does not jump. The first image on a page loads eagerly with fetchpriority="high", since it is usually the largest thing on the screen. Every later image gets loading="lazy" decoding="async". alt and every other attribute of your image are kept. The plugin never writes an alt for you. The variants land in public/_img/, with a hash of the source and the settings in each name, so a URL changes only when the image does. The variants carry no EXIF, GPS or ICC data: the plugin applies the EXIF orientation and then strips all of it. On the plugin's field-test site, a German/English blog, the 32 content images went from 4.2 MB of originals to 0.45 MB of AVIF a phone downloads. The plugin leaves alone what it should not touch: SVG and GIF, external http(s):// URLs, an <img> that already has a srcset or sits inside a <picture>, and any image with ?skip on its URL. An image file that does not exist stays a plain <img>, and the build says so: ⚠️ plugin-images: /pier.html: image not found, left as is: /images/photos/missing.jpg Images in your Pug views are not processed. For those, use frontmatter images and the mixin (step 5). 3. Query parameters Add parameters to the image URL to change one image. The parameters never reach the published URLs. This one is at most 800 pixels wide, cropped to 16:9 around a point 30 % from the left and 60 % from the top: ![The end of the pier](/images/photos/pier.jpg?w=800&ratio=16:9&focus=30,60) <picture> <source type="image/avif" srcset="/_img/pier-7a863ccf-480.avif 480w, /_img/pier-7a863ccf-800.avif 800w, /_img/pier-7a863ccf-1600.avif 1600w" sizes="(min-width: 800px) 800px, 100vw"> <source type="image/webp" srcset="/_img/pier-f3e554c6-480.webp 480w, /_img/pier-f3e554c6-800.webp 800w, /_img/pier-f3e554c6-1600.webp 1600w" sizes="(min-width: 800px) 800px, 100vw"><img src="/_img/pier-85ac4388-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/pier-85ac4388-480.jpg 480w, /_img/pier-85ac4388-800.jpg 800w, /_img/pier-85ac4388-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="(min-width: 800px) 800px, 100vw" width="1600" height="900" alt="The end of the pier" loading="lazy" decoding="async"> </picture> ?w=800 keeps the configured widths below 800, adds 800 and 1600 (for screens with twice the pixel density) and sets a matching sizes. The crop makes the image 1600 × 900. The parameters: Parameter What it does Example w Maximum display width in pixels ?w=800 h Target height; with w it crops ?w=800&h=450 ratio Crop to an aspect ratio ?ratio=16:9 fit cover (the default for a crop), contain or inside ?fit=contain focus Focal point of a crop in percent, or attention / entropy ?focus=30,60 q Quality for all formats, 1–100 ?q=60 formats Modern formats for this image, or none ?formats=webp sizes sizes for this image, URL-encoded ?sizes=50vw loading eager or lazy, overriding the first-image rule ?loading=eager skip Leave this image untouched ?skip A parameter the plugin does not know is ignored with a warning, so a typo does not go unnoticed: ⚠️ plugin-images: /pier.html: unknown parameter "width" ignored: /images/photos/pier.jpg?width=800 4. Captions Give an image a Markdown title, and put it alone in its paragraph: ![The pier at dusk](/images/photos/pier.jpg "Usedom, October 2026") It becomes a <figure> with the title as its caption. The <figure> replaces the paragraph, since a <figure> inside a <p> is invalid HTML: <figure class="nera-image"> <picture> <source type="image/avif" srcset="/_img/pier-1a5869e3-480.avif 480w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-800.avif 800w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-1200.avif 1200w, /_img/pier-1a5869e3-1600.avif 1600w" sizes="100vw"> <source type="image/webp" srcset="/_img/pier-987422b0-480.webp 480w, /_img/pier-987422b0-800.webp 800w, /_img/pier-987422b0-1200.webp 1200w, /_img/pier-987422b0-1600.webp 1600w" sizes="100vw"><img src="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-480.jpg 480w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-800.jpg 800w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1200.jpg 1200w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="100vw" width="1600" height="1200" alt="The pier at dusk" loading="lazy" decoding="async"> </picture> <figcaption class="nera-image__caption">Usedom, October 2026</figcaption> </figure> The same photo as in step 2 reuses the same variants: nothing is encoded twice. An image inline with text, inside a link or next to another image keeps its title and gets no figure. figure: false in config/images.yaml turns captions off. The classes nera-image and nera-image__caption are the plugin's public markup, so style them in your own CSS. 5. Frontmatter images and the +picture mixin A blog post's hero or teaser image usually sits in the frontmatter and is rendered by a view, not by the Markdown. Name it under image: --- layout: pages/post.pug title: A day at the beach description: A post with a hero image image: /images/photos/beach.jpg image_alt: Waves on an empty beach --- # A day at the beach The hero image above comes from the frontmatter. The plugin encodes the variants for it and puts the finished data into meta.images.image: src, srcset, sizes, width, height, the sources per format, and an og crop. meta.image itself stays the string you wrote, so views and plugins that read it keep working. Query parameters work here too (image: /images/photos/beach.jpg?ratio=16:9). More keys than image go into frontmatter_keys in config/images.yaml. The mixin nera add published renders the entry: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main include /vendor/plugin-images/picture +picture(meta.images && meta.images.image, { alt: meta.image_alt, loading: 'eager' }) != content <picture> <source type="image/avif" srcset="/_img/beach-04a0334d-480.avif 480w, /_img/beach-04a0334d-800.avif 800w, /_img/beach-04a0334d-1200.avif 1200w, /_img/beach-04a0334d-1600.avif 1600w" sizes="100vw" /> <source type="image/webp" srcset="/_img/beach-2fc7c78b-480.webp 480w, /_img/beach-2fc7c78b-800.webp 800w, /_img/beach-2fc7c78b-1200.webp 1200w, /_img/beach-2fc7c78b-1600.webp 1600w" sizes="100vw" /><img src="/_img/beach-376379b1-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/beach-376379b1-480.jpg 480w, /_img/beach-376379b1-800.jpg 800w, /_img/beach-376379b1-1200.jpg 1200w, /_img/beach-376379b1-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="100vw" width="1600" height="1200" alt="Waves on an empty beach" loading="eager" fetchpriority="high" /> </picture> A page without the frontmatter key renders nothing there. The mixin's options are alt, class, sizes and loading (lazy by default; eager adds fetchpriority="high"). A hero above the content is the page's largest image, so render it with loading: 'eager' as above, and set eager_first: false in config/images.yaml, so the first Markdown image below it does not compete for the same priority. og:image The og entry is a 1200 × 630 JPEG, the size link previews in social networks and chat apps expect. og:image must be an absolute URL, so set your origin in config/app.yaml: origin: https://example.com and add the tags inside the layout's head, after the other meta tags: if meta.images && meta.images.image && meta.images.image.og - const og = meta.images.image.og meta(property="og:image" content=`${app.origin}${app.basePath || ''}${og.src}`) meta(property="og:image:width" content=og.width) meta(property="og:image:height" content=og.height) public/beach.html then has: <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/_img/beach-a82641dd-1200.jpg" /> <meta property="og:image:width" content="1200" /> <meta property="og:image:height" content="630" /> app.basePath is there for a site served from a subfolder: core rewrites href and src for base_path, but not the content of a <meta>. 6. Placeholders While an image loads, its box is empty. A placeholder fills it: placeholder: color sets the image's dominant colour as its background: <img src="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-480.jpg 480w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-800.jpg 800w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1200.jpg 1200w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="100vw" width="1600" height="1200" style="background-color:#383898" alt="The pier at dusk, seen from the beach" loading="eager" fetchpriority="high"> placeholder: blur sets a tiny blurred WebP instead, inline in the page: <img src="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg" srcset="/_img/pier-10e7e41a-480.jpg 480w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-800.jpg 800w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1200.jpg 1200w, /_img/pier-10e7e41a-1600.jpg 1600w" sizes="100vw" width="1600" height="1200" style="background-image:url(data:image/webp;base64,UklGRkIAAABXRUJQVlA4IDYAAACwAQCdASoQAAwAAsBMJbACdAEOtNWAAP7xfmtUemnWsBu+y/mBlsjTsVhsr/7FRn95mxzwAAA=);background-size:cover" alt="The pier at dusk, seen from the beach" loading="eager" fetchpriority="high"> The build reports them: 🖼️ plugin-images: 4 image(s), 0 variant(s) encoded, 3 placeholder(s) computed Both work for Markdown images and for frontmatter images (the mixin renders the style). An image with transparency gets none, because the background would stay visible through it. The default is none, because a placeholder is an inline style attribute, which a Content Security Policy without 'unsafe-inline' in style-src blocks. A value the plugin does not know, or a key it does not know, warns and falls back to the default; neither fails the build: ⚠️ plugin-images: config/images.yaml: invalid placeholder "smudge", using "none" ⚠️ plugin-images: config/images.yaml: ignoring unknown key "width" 7. Keep your originals off the server The variants are clean, but by default the original is still published: in step 2, public/images/photos/pier.jpg is the 4 MB file with its camera and GPS data, reachable by anyone who guesses the URL. The plugin reads images from the assets folder regardless of .neraignore, so list the photo folder there: images/photos The paths are relative to the assets folder. After the next build, public/ has no images/ folder at all; the pages still show every photo, from public/_img/. The originals stay in your repository. Check first what else lives in that folder. .neraignore matches exact paths and folder prefixes, no glob patterns, and everything in a listed folder the plugin does not process is no longer published: SVGs, GIFs, files you link for download, and images your views use directly, such as an img(src=meta.image) or an og:image built from meta.image. Render those from meta.images (step 5). A folder that holds only photos for your pages is the safe case. nera build --check looks at the built public/, for third-party requests among other things; the CLI reference describes the checks. For this site it reports: ✓ No problems found. 8. The cache, locally and in CI Encoding AVIF is slow. The plugin therefore keeps every variant in .nera-cache/images/ and encodes only what is missing. With the test site's four images (three on the pier page, the hero of the beach post), a build with an empty cache reports: 🖼️ plugin-images: 4 image(s), 34 variant(s) encoded and took 5.3 seconds; the next build: 🖼️ plugin-images: 4 image(s), 0 variant(s) encoded took 0.9. On a site with a hundred photos, a cold build takes a minute or more. Variants no page uses any more are removed from the cache (prune: true). nera new lists .nera-cache in the site's .gitignore (since @nera-static/nera 1.4.1), so the cache never lands in your repository. In CI, keep it between runs instead. The deploy workflow nera publish writes already does that (since @nera-static/nera 1.22.0). In a workflow of your own, add this step before npm run build: - uses: actions/cache@v6 with: path: .nera-cache key: nera-cache-${{ hashFiles('assets/**', 'theme/assets/**', 'pages/**', 'config/images.yaml', 'package-lock.json') }} restore-keys: nera-cache- The key covers pages/** because pages ask for variants (query parameters, frontmatter images), and package-lock.json because a theme from npm brings its own images. actions/cache saves nothing when the key matches exactly, so a key that misses one of them leaves new variants unsaved, and every build encodes them again. 9. Requirements The plugin needs @nera-static/core 4.13.0 or later: it hands its variants to core through the getAssets hook, which copies them into public/. Every current @nera-static/nera brings a newer core. On an older core the build stops, rather than publish pages that link to images which were never copied. With core 4.12.0: ❌ plugin-images: @nera-static/core 4.12.0 is too old; this plugin needs >= 4.13.0 (the getAssets hook). Without it, pages would link to image files that are never copied to public/. Update with `npm update @nera-static/nera` (or `@nera-static/core`). The build exits with code 1. The encoding runs on sharp, a native module. It installs a prebuilt binary for your platform (macOS, Linux and Windows, on x64 and arm64), and the site's package-lock.json lists the binaries of every platform as optional dependencies, so npm ci on a Linux CI runner picks its own even when the lockfile was written on a Mac. Do not install with --omit=optional, which leaves the binary out. The plugin needs Node.js 20.18.1 or later. The plugin's README and npm page have every config key with its default. Next How this website is built shows the plugins of this site working together.

title: Reusable content blocks with plugin-stacks
description: Write sections once in Markdown and place them in any view with plugin-stacks, as single blocks or as ordered, per-language stack groups.
content: Some content belongs to no single page: a call to action under every article, a newsletter box, the feature grid on a homepage. @nera-static/plugin-stacks lets you write such a block once, as a Markdown file in pages/, and place it in any view through app.stacks. Several blocks that form one section become a stack group, ordered and split by language. 1. Install npx nera add stacks nera add installs the package and publishes its default template into theme/views/vendor/plugin-stacks/ (section 4). It copies no config file, as the plugin needs none: stacks are defined in frontmatter. Nera finds the plugin on its own. 2. What makes a page a stack A stack is a Markdown file under pages/ whose frontmatter sets type: stack and a slug or a title. Where the file lives does not matter. A pages/stacks/ folder simply keeps the blocks together: --- type: stack title: Newsletter signup --- Get **one email a month** with what changed. Note what is missing: layout. Nera writes a page to public/ only if its frontmatter has a layout, so a stack without one stays a fragment that other pages embed, not a page of its own. nera validate and nera build --check know this: since @nera-static/validate 1.6.1 they no longer warn layout-missing for a page with type: stack. 3. Use a single stack Every stack lands in app.stacks, keyed by its slug, with the same { content, meta } shape as a page: content is the rendered HTML, meta the whole frontmatter. Without an explicit slug, the key is the title lowercased, with spaces replaced by underscores: Newsletter signup becomes newsletter_signup. Place it in a view, guarded so a missing stack does not break the page: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content if app.stacks.newsletter_signup aside.newsletter!= app.stacks.newsletter_signup.content The aside then holds <p>Get <strong>one email a month</strong> with what changed.</p>. Only spaces are replaced: a title with punctuation produces a key that dot access cannot read. Set an explicit slug for such titles, or whenever you want a key that does not change when the title does. Slugs are one namespace for the whole site; if two stacks end up with the same one, the later one wins and the plugin warns. 4. Render a stack through a template A stack can bring its own markup. nera add already published the plugin's default template to theme/views/vendor/plugin-stacks/stack-template.pug. Point a stack at it with stack_layout, a path from the project root (where you run nera build), not from the views folder: --- type: stack slug: call_to_action title: Ready to start? description: One command scaffolds a site. stack_layout: theme/views/vendor/plugin-stacks/stack-template.pug --- Run `npx @nera-static/nera new my-site` and you are live in minutes. app.stacks.call_to_action.content now holds the template's output, not the bare Markdown: <section class="stack"> <header class="stack__header"> <h2 class="stack__title">Ready to start?</h2> <p class="stack__description">One command scaffolds a site.</p> </header> <article class="stack__content"> <p>Run <code>npx @nera-static/nera new my-site</code> and you are live in minutes.</p> </article> </section> The template reads the stack as stack.meta and stack.content, so you can edit your copy or write your own. The BEM classes are the plugin's public contract: style them from your CSS. Publishing skips a folder that already exists, so after a plugin update npx nera-stacks --force fetches the new template and overwrites your edits. 5. Stack groups A feature grid is a list of blocks. Give each block its own stack page, put them into the same stack_group, and set their order with stack_order: --- type: stack stack_group: home_features stack_order: 1 lang: en title: Markdown in, HTML out --- Author content in Markdown with YAML frontmatter. The plugin then adds two keys: app.stackGroups[<group>] — every stack of the group, in order. app.stackGroupsByLang[<group>][<lang>] — the same, split by lang. A stack without lang counts as the site's app.lang. Each entry is { content, meta } again, so a view loops over it: - const features = app.stackGroupsByLang?.home_features?.[meta.lang || app.lang] || [] each feature in features .feature h2.feature__title #{ feature.meta.title } .feature__body!= feature.content On a single-language site, each feature in app.stackGroups.home_features || [] is enough. Stacks with a numeric stack_order come first, ascending; the rest follow in build order. A grouped stack needs neither a slug nor a title, and it stays out of app.stacks unless it sets an explicit slug. In a test site with three grouped stacks, of which only one had a slug: feature_plugins, app.stacks held exactly that one next to the two ungrouped stacks: call_to_action, feature_plugins, newsletter_signup. That keeps the same section in three languages from colliding on title-derived keys. 6. A real example: this site's feature grid The four boxes on the nera.js.org homepage are a stack group. Each box is one file in pages/stacks/home-features/, with translations in pages/de/stacks/home-features/ and pages/es/stacks/home-features/: --- type: stack stack_group: home_features stack_order: 1 lang: en title: Markdown in, HTML out --- Author content in Markdown with YAML frontmatter. Nera renders each page through a Pug layout you control and writes plain, fast HTML. The homepage view picks the boxes for the current language and numbers them from their position in the list: - const features = app.stackGroupsByLang?.home_features?.[curLang] || [] if features.length .home-body__grid each feature, i in features .home-body__feature p.home-body__feature-num #{ String(i + 1).padStart(2, '0') } h2.home-body__feature-title #{ feature.meta.title } .home-body__feature-desc!= feature.content curLang is set in the site's base layout from meta.lang. Adding a fifth box is one new Markdown file per language, with no change to the view. 7. Pitfall: stack pages are still pages A stack has no layout, so it is never built, but it stays in the page list every other plugin sees. In a test site with stacks in pages/stacks/, the plugins behaved like this: plugin sees stack pages? what to do plugin-search no — pages without layout are left out of the index nothing plugin-page-pagination no — a page without layout is never a previous/next target nothing plugin-navigation no — it lists only the hrefs in config/navigation.yaml nothing plugin-statistics yes — it counts every Markdown file under pages/ keep the counted keys (tags, category, …) off stack pages plugin-simple-page-list yes — with page_path: /stacks, it listed every stack with an href like /stacks/newsletter.html that was never built keep stacks out of listed folders, or exclude them with exclude_pages The exclude_pages entries use the stack's would-be page URL: page_path: /blog exclude_pages: - /blog/newsletter.html A folder of its own, like pages/stacks/, is the simpler fix: no listed path matches it, so nothing needs excluding. Next How this website is built shows how plugin-stacks works together with the other plugins on this site. To merge whole sections into one scrolling page instead, see Build a one-page site.

title: Tag your content and get topic pages for free
description: Add tags to pages with plugin-tags and get auto-generated tag overview pages and a tag cloud.
content: @nera-static/plugin-tags reads a tags: field from your frontmatter, then builds a browsable overview page for every tag automatically. 1. Install and publish templates npx nera add tags nera add installs the package, copies its default config/tags.yaml into your site and publishes the templates into theme/views/vendor/plugin-tags/. 2. Tag some pages Add a comma-separated tags value to any page's frontmatter: --- layout: pages/tutorial.pug title: Add client-side search tags: plugins, search --- Tags are slugified and case-folded, so Web Dev, web dev and WEB DEV all map to one page at /tags/web-dev.html. 3. Configure config/tags.yaml, the file nera add copied, sets every key to its default, so it changes nothing until you edit it; the keys commented out in it are examples. These are the first four: meta_property_name: tags tag_overview_path: '/tags' tag_separator: ',' tag_overview_layout: pages/default.pug tag_overview_layout is the layout every generated tag page renders with. Point it at a layout that renders the published overview template: tag_overview_layout: pages/tag-overview.pug Then create theme/views/pages/tag-overview.pug: extends ../layouts/layout block content .container include ../vendor/plugin-tags/pages/tag-overview 4. Show tags on a page The plugin gives each page a meta.tagLinks list. Include the published partial in your article layout: if meta.tagLinks include ../vendor/plugin-tags/partials/tag-links And for a site-wide cloud, app.tagCloud drives the tag-cloud partial: if app.tagCloud include ../vendor/plugin-tags/partials/tag-cloud 5. Per-language tags (optional) By default every tag lives in one namespace, so a multilingual site merges all languages into one overview page. Set group_by_lang to give each language its own: group_by_lang: true Tags are then collected per meta.lang, and the language code prefixes the whole tag_overview_path. With tag_overview_path: '/tutorials/tags' you get: /tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # default language /de/tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # German pages only /es/tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # Spanish pages only The default language stays unprefixed, which is what you want when it is served from the root. If every language sits in its own directory, set prefix_default_lang: true so it gets a segment too. Pages without a meta.lang fall into the default language rather than a bucket of their own, so a single-language site is unaffected by any of this. Chips and clouds follow along on their own: meta.tagLinks links within the page's own language, and each page gets a meta.tagCloud scoped to it. Watch one detail — app.tagCloud still exists, but with grouping on it holds the default language's cloud. Guarding on it is fine; reading it directly to render a cloud is not, because a German page would show English tags. The shipped tag-cloud partial already prefers meta.tagCloud and falls back to app.tagCloud, so use the partial rather than looping yourself. app.tagCloudByLang has every language, keyed by code, if you need them all at once. Generated overview pages also carry their own meta.lang, so t() inside the overview layout resolves in that page's language. Render, and every tag now has its own page — no manual index maintenance. The tutorial you're reading is tagged this way; the chips above link to the generated tag pages. This site runs with group_by_lang: true, so those chips lead to the tag pages for whichever language you are reading.

title: Use and customise a theme
description: Start a site from an installable theme, change its colours, CSS and markup file by file, keep receiving the theme's updates through npm, and switch a blog between the four blog themes.
content: A Nera theme is an npm package: layouts, page types, partials, a stylesheet and a set of design tokens. Your site does not copy it. It installs the package and puts a file of its own next to it only where it wants something different. Every other file still comes from the package, so npm update keeps bringing the theme's fixes, like a child theme in WordPress. This tutorial uses @nera-static/theme-business, the theme of the business and portfolio starters. You change a colour, add a few CSS rules, replace one partial, update the theme, and add a theme to a site that has none. Then a blog switches between the four blog themes. Every command and output below was run in a fresh site with theme-business 1.0.3, @nera-static/nera 1.29.0 and @nera-static/core 4.19.1; section 9 in a blog from --starter blog with theme-blog 2.1.0, theme-stack 2.2.0, theme-ansitz 1.1.0 and theme-umwege 1.1.1. 1. Start a site with a theme npx @nera-static/nera new my-site --theme business cd my-site 📦 Creating a new Nera site in …/my-site... ✓ Configured project as "my-site" ✓ Using theme "business" (@nera-static/theme-business) • pages/imprint.md and pages/privacy.md are placeholders: link them from the theme's layout (theme-blog and theme-business take `footer_links` in config/theme.yaml), or `nera build --check` keeps warning legal-imprint-link and legal-privacy-link. --theme business does two things. It adds the package to package.json: "dependencies": { "@nera-static/nera": "^1.29.0", "@nera-static/theme-business": "^1.0.3" } and it names the theme in config/app.yaml: theme: business business is short for @nera-static/theme-business. The site gets no layout of its own: theme/ holds only empty folders (views/layouts/, views/pages/ and assets/), and every view comes from the package in node_modules/. Want sample pages for services, opening hours and contact as well? The business starter brings the same theme with them: npx @nera-static/nera new my-site --starter business. 2. Make the first build clean Build with the output checks: npx nera build --check public/imprint.html :44 warning page has more than one `<h1>` — one main heading per page keeps its outline clear; keep one and make the others `<h2>` (WCAG 1.3.1, best practice) (on 3 pages, e.g. public/imprint.html, public/index.html, public/privacy.html) a11y-h1 :33 warning page has no link whose text names the imprint (Impressum, Imprint, Legal notice) — it should be easy to find and directly reachable from every page; link it from the layout, such as in the footer, or, if it is linked under another name, set `legal.imprint` in config/validate.yaml (§ 5 DDG) (on 3 pages, e.g. public/imprint.html, public/index.html, public/privacy.html) legal-imprint-link :33 warning page has no link whose text names the privacy policy (Datenschutz, Privacy, Data protection) — it should be easy to find and directly reachable from every page; link it from the layout, such as in the footer, or, if it is linked under another name, set `legal.privacy` in config/validate.yaml (Art. 13 DSGVO) (on 3 pages, e.g. public/imprint.html, public/index.html, public/privacy.html) legal-privacy-link 0 error(s), 3 warning(s) Both come from the scaffolded pages, not from the theme: The theme renders the page's title as its one <h1>, so a page's Markdown starts at ##. Delete the # Welcome to Nera, # Imprint and # Privacy lines from the three pages. The footer links the legal pages you list. Create the site's own config/theme.yaml: footer_links: - label: Imprint href: /imprint.html - label: Privacy href: /privacy.html Build again: ✓ No problems found. The footer now carries: <nav class="site-footer__legal" aria-label="Legal"><a href="/imprint.html">Imprint</a><a href="/privacy.html">Privacy</a></nav> Replace the two placeholder pages with your own texts before you publish. 3. How a theme and your site share the work Nera looks for every view and every asset in two places, your site first: what your site the theme package views theme/views/<path> node_modules/@nera-static/theme-business/views/<path> assets theme/assets/<path> node_modules/@nera-static/theme-business/assets/<path> settings config/theme.yaml the package's config/theme.yaml A file in your site wins over the theme's file of the same path, and only that one file. Everything you do not override comes from the package. Assets are copied theme first, then your site's, so public/ ends up with both, and yours on top. Your config/theme.yaml is merged key by key over the theme's defaults: you set only what you change (lists such as footer_links are replaced as a whole). The theme's README has a table of what to change where. From cheapest to most expensive: to change do this you keep theme updates for a colour, a font, a width a token in config/theme.yaml everything a few CSS rules theme/assets/css/custom.css + extra_css everything one partial or page type copy it to theme/views/<same path> every other file the whole page shell override layouts/layout.pug page types, partials, CSS Sections 4 to 6 go down this table. 4. Change a colour Every token in the theme's config/theme.yaml becomes a CSS custom property: tokens.color.accent becomes --theme-color-accent. Change the accent (links, buttons, the top rule) to a dark teal and give the focus outline the old rust colour: tokens: color: accent: '#1c5f74' focus: '#a1400f' footer_links: - label: Imprint href: /imprint.html - label: Privacy href: /privacy.html After npx nera build, the <style> the theme writes into every page's <head> carries your values next to the defaults you did not touch: <style> :root { --theme-color-bg: #fbf2e3; --theme-color-surface: #f1e0c3; --theme-color-text: #3b2314; --theme-color-muted: #6e4b2e; --theme-color-accent: #1c5f74; --theme-color-accent-text: #ffffff; --theme-color-border: #dcc6a3; --theme-color-focus: #a1400f; … } </style> Keep the contrast when you change colours: the accent is text on the page background and on cards, and the background of buttons. #1c5f74 reaches 6.4:1 on the background, 5.5:1 on the card colour and 7.1:1 under white button text, all above the 4.5:1 that WCAG asks for. The theme's README lists every token and every colour pair it checks. 5. Add your own CSS For rules the tokens do not cover, add a stylesheet of your own and let the theme link it. Put it into theme/assets/css/custom.css; the rule styles a line you will add in the next section: .page-kicker { margin: 0 0 0.25rem; color: var(--theme-color-accent); font-size: 0.875rem; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: 0.08em; text-transform: uppercase; } and list it under extra_css in config/theme.yaml: extra_css: - /css/custom.css The theme links it after its own stylesheet and the token <style>, so your rules win: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/theme.css"> <style> … </style> <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/custom.css"> public/css/ now holds both theme.css (from the package) and custom.css (from your site). Use the tokens (var(--theme-color-accent)) rather than copied colour values, so a change in section 4 reaches your rules too. The theme lists its public class names in its README; those are the ones that stay stable across minor and patch releases. Do not override theme/assets/css/theme.css itself: your copy would replace the theme's whole stylesheet, and its fixes would stop reaching you. 6. Override one partial Now change markup. The page header of every page except the front page lives in the partial partials/page-header.pug. Copy it from the package to the same path in your site: mkdir -p theme/views/partials cp node_modules/@nera-static/theme-business/views/partials/page-header.pug theme/views/partials/ and add a small line above the title, read from a new kicker frontmatter key: //- Overrides the theme's partials/page-header.pug: adds a kicker line //- above the page title, from the page's `kicker` frontmatter. header.page__header if meta.kicker p.page-kicker= meta.kicker h1.page__title= meta.title || app.name if meta.lead p.page__lead= meta.lead The class is your own, page-kicker, not a name inside the theme's page__… block: a later theme release could add a page__kicker of its own. Use it on a page: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: About us kicker: Since 1998 lead: A small bakery in the middle of Berlin. description: Who we are and how we bake --- ## Our story We bake every loaf by hand. npx nera build renders public/about.html with your header: <header class="page__header"> <p class="page-kicker">Since 1998</p> <h1 class="page__title">About us</h1> <p class="page__lead">A small bakery in the middle of Berlin.</p> </header> A page without kicker renders as before. Every other view, the layout, the footer, the page types, still comes from the package: you took over one file, not the theme. A theme often prepares such places for you. theme-business ships empty partials, its seams, for plugin output: partials/head-extra.pug at the end of <head>, partials/nav-main.pug in the header navigation, partials/footer-extra.pug in the footer and a few more, listed in its README. Overriding a seam costs nothing, since there is no theme markup in it to miss out on. For a page type of your own, put a new file under theme/views/pages/ that extends ../layouts/layout.pug; the README shows one. 7. Updates keep coming Update the theme the same way as Nera itself: npx nera update 🔄 Updating Nera packages: @nera-static/nera, @nera-static/theme-business nera update runs npm update for every @nera-static/ package in package.json, the theme included. Like npm update, it stays within each package's range, so a new major version of the theme is never installed behind your back. npm ls shows the version you have: npm ls @nera-static/theme-business my-site@1.0.0 …/my-site └── @nera-static/theme-business@1.0.3 An update replaces the files in node_modules/, never the ones in your theme/. That cuts both ways: Your tokens, custom.css and page-header.pug survive every update. Your page-header.pug no longer receives the theme's changes to that file. Everything else does. After an update, compare each file you override with the theme's new version and take over what you want: diff node_modules/@nera-static/theme-business/views/partials/page-header.pug theme/views/partials/page-header.pug 1,2c1,2 < //- The page header of every page type but home (§S3.1 "Header"): the page's < //- one <h1> and its lead. --- > //- Overrides the theme's partials/page-header.pug: adds a kicker line > //- above the page title, from the page's `kicker` frontmatter. 3a4,5 > if meta.kicker > p.page-kicker= meta.kicker Here the only differences are yours. The theme follows semantic versioning over its view paths, tokens, settings and public classes: a minor or patch release keeps your overrides working, and a major one says in its CHANGELOG what to change. The fewer files you override, the less there is to compare. 8. Add a theme to an existing site A site created without --theme has its own layout, scaffolded by nera new. Install the theme and name it in config/app.yaml: npm install @nera-static/theme-business theme: business nera validate then points at the two scaffolded views that are in the way: theme/views/layouts/layout.pug :1 warning the `nera new` starter file hides the theme's own layouts/layout.pug — delete it to use the theme's, or remove the `nera:scaffold-default` line to keep it on purpose theme-shadowed theme/views/pages/default.pug :1 warning the `nera new` starter file hides the theme's own pages/default.pug — delete it to use the theme's, or remove the `nera:scaffold-default` line to keep it on purpose theme-shadowed 0 error(s), 2 warning(s) They have the same paths as two of the theme's views, so by the rule of section 3 they would win, and the theme would never show. Their first line, //- nera:scaffold-default, marks them as untouched starter files. Delete them: rm theme/views/layouts/layout.pug theme/views/pages/default.pug npx nera validate ✓ No problems found. If you changed one of them and want to keep it, remove its nera:scaffold-default line instead: the file is then a deliberate override and the warning goes away. Then fix the headings and the footer links as in section 2. A page renders with the theme's page type of the same name as its layout. theme-business has pages/home.pug, default.pug, contact.pug, list.pug and gallery.pug; a page whose layout names a view neither your site nor the theme has fails nera validate with layout-unresolved, which names both places it looked. 9. Switch between the blog themes Four themes are made for blogs: @nera-static/theme-blog ("Plain"), theme-stack for code, theme-ansitz for photographs and theme-umwege for travel. The demos show each with its starter's sample posts: Plain, Stack, Ansitz and Umwege. The four share one contract, so a blog written for one renders in each of the others. Start one with the plain blog: npx @nera-static/nera new my-blog --starter blog --yes cd my-blog With --yes, --starter blog takes the plain blog without asking: the site depends on @nera-static/theme-blog ^2.1.0, and config/app.yaml says theme: blog. What the four themes share: shared keys page types pages/home.pug, post.pug, archive.pug, tag.pug, default.pug config/theme.yaml author.name, author.bio, author.href, blog.home_posts, blog.featured_series, blog.highlight_tag, blog.post_layouts, footer_links, extra_css post frontmatter date, updated, author, image, image_alt, tags, series, series_part, facts, location, image_note the rest the seams for plugin output and the t() keys To switch to Stack, install the package: npm install @nera-static/theme-stack added 1 package, and audited 168 packages in 833ms and change the one line in config/app.yaml: theme: stack npx nera build --check ✓ No problems found. The same pages, the same config/theme.yaml and every file the starter put into theme/ now render in Stack. theme: ansitz and theme: umwege (after npm install @nera-static/theme-ansitz @nera-static/theme-umwege) build just as clean. Once you have chosen, remove the packages you no longer use: npm uninstall @nera-static/theme-blog. What a theme does not draw, it ignores, so switching never breaks a page: location and image_note appear in Ansitz (both) and Umwege (location); Plain and Stack show neither. Give the starter's post pages/posts/tags.md a location: Berlin, and its page carries <p class="post__location"> under Ansitz and Umwege and nothing under Plain and Stack, with a clean build in all four. blog.highlight_tag is a list on the home in Plain, Ansitz and Umwege; Stack renders nothing for it. blog.featured_series is a block on the home in Plain, Stack and Ansitz; Umwege renders nothing for it. blog.home_posts counts the posts the home lists after its large opening, which is never counted: the "Latest post" in Plain and Stack, the boarding pass in Umwege (both the newest post), and the hero in Ansitz (the newest post with an image). Each theme has a default that fills its own grid (Plain 9, Stack 6, Ansitz and Umwege 7). Set it in your config/theme.yaml and it applies to whichever theme you use: with home_posts: 2, "Recent posts" lists two posts in all four. Two things deserve a look when you switch: Tokens are each theme's own. The eight colour tokens (bg, surface, text, muted, accent, accent_text, border, focus) exist in all four, so colours you set carry over, but they were chosen for another look: drop them, or check their contrast again (section 4). Stack and Umwege have a few tokens of their own (Stack's night, night_text, night_muted and highlight, Umwege's sun, coral and sky). Your files in theme/views/ stay and win over every theme. The starter's seams (partials/post-media.pug, tag-cloud.pug and the others), its search page type pages/search.pug and its vendor copies rendered unchanged under all four themes. An override of a theme's own view, like the page-header.pug of section 6, is a copy of one theme's file: compare it with the new theme's file of the same path (section 7) before you keep it. Stack, Ansitz and Umwege are wider than Plain; their READMEs suggest wider widths for @nera-static/plugin-images in config/images.yaml. 10. Build your own theme A theme of your own is an npm package with the same layout: views/, assets/ and config/theme.yaml. @nera-static/theme-example is the smallest one, kept small to copy: its README's section Using it as a blueprint for your own theme walks through renaming the package, the fields Nera needs to find it, and the seams that let a site extend it without forking. theme-business shows the same ideas at full size: tokens, seams and a documented contract. Next The theme-business README has every token, setting, seam and public class. The plugin tutorials, such as Custom navigation, show how to publish a plugin's templates; with theme-business you include them from a seam, as its README shows for each plugin it supports. The READMEs of theme-blog, theme-stack, theme-ansitz and theme-umwege say what each blog theme draws from the shared keys.

title: Write your own local plugin
description: Build a project-local plugin that adds data to app with the getAppData hook and writes a file into public/ with the getAssets hook.
content: You don't need to publish to npm to extend Nera. Any module at src/plugins/<name>/index.js is discovered and applied automatically — that is the default, and a site made with nera new has no setting for it. To keep local plugins elsewhere, set folders.plugins in config/app.yaml — this site uses plugins/: folders: plugins: ./plugins Let's build a real one: a plugin that collects every tutorial into a list for an index page — a simplified version of the plugin that powers this site — and then publishes the same list as tutorials.json. The contract A plugin exports any of three hooks: export function getAppData({ app, pagesData }) { // must return a plain object — becomes the new `app` } export function getMetaData({ app, pagesData }) { // must return an array — becomes the new `pagesData` } export function getAssets({ app, pagesData }) { // must return an array of { from, to } — files core copies into public/ } getAppData runs first; getMetaData sees the app it returned. getAssets (core ≥ 4.13.0) runs once every plugin is done with the other two. Nera awaits all hooks (since core 4.3.0; older versions silently replaced app with a Promise), but synchronous stays the safe default — it is what the published plugins do. A hook that returns the wrong type does not stop the build: core prints a warning such as ⚠️ Plugin "tutorials-list" getAppData returned invalid format, skipping replace. and keeps the old data. When a plugin seems to do nothing, read the build log first. "The hook contract" in the plugin docs has the short version. Build it Create src/plugins/tutorials-list/index.js: export function getAppData({ app, pagesData }) { if (!app || typeof app !== 'object') return app if (!Array.isArray(pagesData)) return app const tutorials = pagesData .filter(({ meta }) => { const href = meta?.href || '' return href.startsWith('/tutorials/') && href !== '/tutorials/index.html' }) .map(({ meta }) => ({ href: meta.href, title: meta.title || meta.href, description: meta.description || '', createdAt: meta.createdAt, })) .sort((a, b) => { const da = new Date(a.createdAt).getTime() const db = new Date(b.createdAt).getTime() if (!Number.isNaN(da) && !Number.isNaN(db) && da !== db) return db - da return String(a.href).localeCompare(String(b.href)) }) return { ...app, tutorials } } That's the whole plugin. It reads every page, keeps the ones under /tutorials/, and returns a new app with a sorted tutorials array. Use it in a layout app.tutorials is now available in every view: if app.tutorials && app.tutorials.length ul.tutorials__list each post in app.tutorials li.tutorials__item a.tutorials__link(href=post.href) h2 #{ post.title } p #{ post.description } Hand over a file with getAssets Now publish the same list as /tutorials.json. Writing it into public/ from a hook does not work: plugins run before core deletes and re-creates public/, so the file is gone by the end of the build. Write it into .nera-cache/tutorials-list/ instead (nera new puts .nera-cache in .gitignore) and return it from getAssets. Add this to the same file: import fs from 'fs' import path from 'path' // getAppData from above stays as it is export function getAssets({ app }) { if (!Array.isArray(app?.tutorials)) return [] const dir = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.nera-cache/tutorials-list') const from = path.join(dir, 'tutorials.json') fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true }) fs.writeFileSync(from, `${JSON.stringify(app.tutorials, null, 4)}\n`) return [{ from, to: 'tutorials.json' }] } Each entry is { from, to }: from is an absolute path to a file or folder, to a path relative to public/ — the target file for a file, the folder its contents go into for a folder ('' is public/ itself). getAssets sees the final app, so app.tutorials from your own getAppData is already there. After nera build, public/tutorials.json holds the list, newest first: [ { "href": "/tutorials/second.html", "title": "Second tutorial", "description": "The newer one.", "createdAt": "2026-08-01T00:00:00.000Z" }, { "href": "/tutorials/first.html", "title": "First tutorial", "description": "The older one.", "createdAt": "2026-07-01T00:00:00.000Z" } ] Core copies the files in the order theme → plugins → site, so a file of the same name in your own theme/assets/ still wins. The copy happens before base_path and asset hashing, so both cover plugin files too. An entry with a relative from or a to outside public/ is skipped with a warning, such as ⚠️ Plugin "tutorials-list" getAssets entry skipped: "from" must be an absolute path (…). For real-world examples, see this site's llms-txt and skill-zip plugins. Why return a new object Nera threads each hook's return value into the next. Returning { ...app, tutorials } (rather than mutating app) keeps that data flow predictable — the same reason the built-in plugins do it. From here, the same pattern builds related-posts lists, author pages, "recently updated" widgets — anything derived from your content.
